summary_html: An intake **screen** is elevated to a formal **investigation/assessment** under state criteria. CAPTA and CFSR establish the federal expectations for screening, timelines, and investigative quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening/investigation conditions for funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review framework

primary_citations.citation_text: New York - N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 411 et seq. (Child Protective Services Act – reporting requirements)
New York - Family Court Act Article 10 (Abuse/Neglect juvenile proceedings)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Matter of Lee TT. v. Dowling
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals held that the 'some credible evidence' standard for retaining an indicated report in the Statewide Central Register violates federal due process to the extent the report is disseminated to provider and licensing agencies, and that a subject is entitled to a pre-deprivation hearing at which the agency must prove the abuse or maltreatment by a fair preponderance of the evidence.
key_cases.relevance: The decision describes the statutory test for transmitting a hotline report to the local agency for investigation.
key_cases.quote: subjects are entitled to a predeprivation hearing to determine by a fair preponderance of the evidence whether reports of abuse can be substantiated and relevant to future employment or licensure

key_cases.case_name: Matter of Catherine G. v. County of Essex
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a fourteen-year-old sibling is not a 'person legally responsible' under Family Court Act § 1012, so mandated reporters had no statutory duty to report his abuse of his sisters and the mother's late notice of claim against county and school officials was patently meritless.
key_cases.relevance: The opinion shows the hotline's screening criteria determining whether a report is transmitted for investigation.
key_cases.quote: When in doubt about whether a case must be reported under Social Services Law § 413, they ought to err on the side of caution and make a report

key_cases.case_name: Southerland v. City of New York
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Second Circuit vacated summary judgment for the caseworker on the father's Fourth Amendment unlawful-search claim and the children's unlawful-seizure and procedural due process claims, holding that a Family Court order obtained on a materially misleading affidavit cannot supply the warrant equivalent and that fact disputes remained over whether emergency circumstances justified the removal.
key_cases.relevance: It shows what a caseworker must actually establish before escalating from a report to a court-authorized home search.
key_cases.quote: In child-abuse investigations, a Family Court order is equivalent to a search warrant for Fourth Amendment purposes

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed confirmation of an indicated Central Register report, holding that there is no constitutional right to assigned counsel at a Statewide Central Register administrative fair hearing and that the 2020 amendments to Social Services Law § 422 - including the fair-preponderance standard and the irrebuttable presumption from an article 10 dismissal - do not apply retroactively to determinations rendered before their January 1, 2022 effective date.
key_cases.relevance: The opinion traces the path from hotline report through local agency investigation to an indicated determination.
key_cases.quote: Inclusion on the SCR—unlike Family Court article 10 proceedings—does not impact rights that we have concluded warrant recognition of a constitutional right to assigned counsel in civil proceedings
